newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia allays mobile phone-cancer link fears.
newsitem.headline: Australia allays mobile phone-cancer link fears.

text.p: The Australian government moved on Wednesday to allay fears of a link between cancer in humans and the use of digital mobile telephones despite research on mice which established a possible connection.

A study by the Royal Adelaide Hospital released on Wednesday showed that cancer rates almost doubled in mice after prolonged exposure to radiofrequency (RF) electromagnetic fields of the type used in mobile phones.
But the Australian government said that, while the research was a useful contribution, the cancer risk on humans of mobile phones was minimal.
"It does not mean that mobile phones pose any significant risk to the health of users," MP Dr Brendan Nelson said in a statement released on behalf of the government.
"Based on current knowledge, any risk attached to mobile phone use is minimal compared with the everyday risks faced from, for example, sunlight and driving our cars," he said.
"We know that one in 35 people will develop skin cancer and that five people are killed every day in car-related accidents.
"We don't know of any one person anywhere in the world who has died as a result of using a mobile phone," said Nelson, a former president of the Australian Medical Association.

Dr Michael Repacholi, chief scientist at the Royal Adelaide Hospital, said the results of his team's study were surprising but further research was needed to determine any conclusive effects on humans.

"This is the first scientific study to show such an effect," Repacholi told a news conference in Adelaide by a video link-up from Geneva, where he is working on a World Health Organisation electromagnetic project.

"We have a lot more research still to do before this result can be used in the debate as to whether electromagnetic fields have any influence on cancer," said Repacholi of the study, funded by Australian telecommunications carrier Telstra.

The study, published on Wednesday in the United States journal Radiation Research, involved 100 mice carrying a cancer-causing gene which made them prone to develop lymphomas -- a cancer of the immune system.
The mice underwent prolonged exposure of an hour each day over 18 months to RF electromagnetic fields of the kind emitted by digital mobile phones.
"Exposure to the RF fields increased the incidence of these tumours from a spontaneous rate of 22 percent to 43 percent over (the period)," Royal Adelaide Hospital said in a statement.
Repacholi said that it could take up to four years before his researchers could confirm the result of the study.
